headline: Antarctic Crossing Goes Fuel-Free With Ancient Kite Design
meta_description: Spanish explorer leads fuel-free Antarctic crossing using kite-powered sled inspired by Inuit tradition, conducting 16 research projects across 3,400 kilometer…
summary_short: A team crossing Antarctica's interior will use zero fuel, powered instead by kites and 25 years of design innovation rooted in Inuit sled-building techniques.
body:
Spanish polar explorer Ramón Larramendi is leading a four-person team across 3,400 kilometers of Antarctic interior using a kite-powered sled that will burn no fuel whatsoever. The Wind Sled expedition, which departed Spain on October 18, replaces the roughly 45,000 gallons of fuel consumed by the last comparable crossing with wind and solar energy. Over an 85-day journey, the crew will conduct 16 research projects selected by Spain's polar research committee, including collaborations with NASA's Ames Research Center and six Spanish universities. One NASA project will investigate whether salt rocks on Antarctica's surface could harbor microbial life—essentially an astrobiology question exploring the extreme limits of where life might exist on Earth.

The sled itself is a synthesis of cutting-edge engineering and ancient tradition. Larramendi spent 25 years developing the platform, logging more than 28,000 kilometers across ice on earlier expeditions while refining it. Built on Inuit sled-building techniques, the 15-meter-long vehicle carries up to 2,100 kilograms and operates with 20 interchangeable kites ranging from 5 to 150 square meters, allowing the crew to adapt to changing wind conditions. Average cruising speed sits around 25 kilometers per hour.

What makes this crossing truly significant is its repeatability. Unlike fuel-based expeditions designed as one-off achievements, this route can be traversed again and again, allowing researchers to compare data across seasons and track real changes in ice, climate, and polar ecosystems over time. When the team reaches Concordia research station at Dome C, they'll leave the sled there, ready for return journeys that will deepen scientific understanding of one of Earth's most isolated and least-studied regions.
quick_facts: Team of four crossing 3,400 km with zero fuel consumption
Sled design developed over 25 years, rooted in Inuit traditions
16 research projects including NASA astrobiology study
20 kites ranging from 5 to 150 square meters for propulsion
